articles.title: President Tinubu to 'pray for Nigeria' during Saudi Arabia trip to Mecca
articles.summary: He last travelled to Mecca in 2022 as he was campaigning to become Nigeria's president.
articles.body:
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is travelling to the holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia to perform the lesser Hajj pilgrimage, known as Umrah, where he will offer prayers for the West African nation, the presidency says.

The visit would provide the 74-year-old president with an opportunity for "spiritual reflection, devotion and prayers for Nigeria's peace, unity, stability and continued progress", his spokesman Bayo Onanuga said.

Tinubu, a Muslim from southern Nigeria, last travelled to Saudi Arabia for Umrah in 2022, while campaigning to become Nigeria's president.

The next election is in January and the country's widespread security challenges have become a major campaign issue.

Why Nigeria's one-time political giant may face extinction

Onanuga's statement said the president would "perform the religious rites associated with Umrah, seeking Allah's guidance and blessings for Nigeria and its people".

Unlike the Hajj, which has fixed dates once a year and is a pilgrimage that Muslims who are able to must perform at least once in their lifetime, Umrah can be performed at any time and involves a shorter set of religious rites.

Meanwhile, Tinubu's media aide Olusegun Dada has dismissed speculation that the real reason for the trip is that the president needs medical checks.

There was widespread discussion about the president's health last weekend after a video went viral on social media appearing to show First Lady Oluremi Tinubu popping something into Tinubu's mouth at the election campaign launch for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) party.

There has been no official comment regarding the incident.

In a post on X, Dada said the president's trip was intended to offer "supplications for the country" and to commit the president's re-election bid "into the hands of God" as he began "another major political journey".

According to a survey by US-based Pew Research Center, more than 90% of Nigerians say religion is "very important" in their lives - one of the highest proportions globally.

Nigeria - Africa's most populous nation - is roughly evenly divided between Christians and Muslims, with a small number of traditional believers.

"It is a regular practice among Muslims when they want to embark on any critical journey or attain a milestone," Dada said, reminding his followers that Tinubu had last done the lesser Hajj ahead of the APC's presidential primary in 2022.

The next elections are scheduled for 16 January when Tinubu's main challengers will again be former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.

As campaigning gets under way the economy and insecurity are major issues for voters.

The country faces an array of security challenges including an Islamist insurgency, attacks by criminal gangs - known locally as "bandits" who loot and kidnap for ransom - clashes over land and separatist unrest.

articles.title: Kevin Bleyer, an Emmy-winning ‘Daily Show’ writer, killed in car crash at 54
articles.summary: Kevin Bleyer, a “The Daily Show” writer, died in a car crash Sunday, his wife said in an Instagram statement.
articles.body: Kevin Bleyer, a “The Daily Show” writer, died in a car crash Sunday, his wife said in an Instagram statement. He was 54. “I am devastated, heartbroken, shattered,” Nella Vera wrote. “My heart has a hole in it that will never be filled,” she posted alongside a picture of him. Bleyer’s family said the accident happened on a rural road in Millrift, Pennsylvania, Variety reported. He had a home in the area. Bleyer worked on “The Daily Show” with Jon Stewart for nine years and an additional eight years as a writer for “Politically Incorrect” with Bill Maher and Dennis Miller. He won four Primetime Emmy Awards, a Writers Guild Award and a Peabody Award for his work. Bleyer wrote speeches for then-President Barack Obama and then-New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio, among others. He also authored books and plays. A graduate of Stanford University, Bleyer also worked globally, including in Kenya, Jordan and Moldova. He briefly lived in Kyrgyzstan where he executive produced “Studio 7,” the first political satire news show in Central Asia, according to his official website. He has also worked as a writer and producer for NBC News’ “TODAY” show and CNN, it added. Bleyer met his wife in 2010 at a production of “Bloody Bloody Andrew Jackson” at the Public Theater, Vera wrote on Instagram. “We became fast friends, bonding over our shared love of political comedy,” she wrote, adding that they had begun dating in 2015 and were married in June 2025. “The last eleven years have had their ups and downs, as life does, but above all, they have been filled with immense love, laughter, dogs, and travel. I was in awe of his intellect, dazzled by his wit, amazed by his fearlessness and spirit of adventure, besotted by his loving heart, and smitten by his beautiful blue eyes,” she wrote. Vera urged the public to donate in her husband’s honor to the Alzheimer’s Association New York City chapter, where she said he had been a volunteer. She hailed his “many public accomplishments ... throughout his long and successful career,” but noted that “to me, he was my soulmate, my partner in crime, and the one who made life so much more fun.”

articles.title: Philippine police obtain warrant to search Thomas Markle's devices
articles.summary: Images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Meghan's father had reportedly been found in his former home in the Philippines.
articles.body:
Philippine police have obtained a warrant to examine devices seized from the former home of Thomas Markle, father of the Duchess of Sussex.

Earlier this month, it was reported that hundreds of images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Thomas Markle Sr, 82, had been found at the property in the Philippines.

Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old videotapes, were handed to police by Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, last week. However, officers in Cebu needed a court warrant before they could examine the items.

Thomas Markle Sr, who is now in the US, has strongly denied the allegations made by his son, describing them as "sick lies".

Cebu Regional Prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that Thomas Markle Jr was "adamant" that the case should be investigated, and that he felt his father "has to answer for it".

Last week, the Sun on Sunday reported that Thomas Markle Sr's ex-wife, Roslyn Loveless, had sent a letter to the Metropolitan Police about the 2019 allegations, which was shared with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex at the time.

Loveless, who has since died, is the mother of Meghan's two half-siblings. She divorced Thomas Markle Sr. in 1975, before he married the duchess's mother.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a statement shared on Friday, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Speaking to the Sun, Thomas Markle Jr also apologised to Meghan for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement, and said he had "been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years".

Thomas Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May.

He is reportedly now living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.

The police say they must identify how the material was obtained before they can consider any criminal charges.

Campaigners describe Cebu as a known hotspot for the sexual exploitation of children, and authorities say they take any such allegations very seriously.

articles.title: Jersey minimum wage increase accepted by minister
articles.summary: A recommendation to increase the minimum wage by 2.8% is agreed by Senator Elaine Millar.
articles.body:
A recommendation to increase the minimum wage has been accepted by the social security minister.

​The Jersey Employment Forum's latest report recommended hiking the minimum wage rate to £13.97 per hour from 1 April 2027 - an increase of 2.8% on the current £13.59 in line with the Jersey retail price index (RPI) in June 2026.

Senator Elaine Millar, Minister for Social Security, said she had "decided to accept the forum's recommendations in respect of the main minimum wage and trainee minimum wage rates".

Forum chairwoman Carla Benest said it had been "challenging times" for businesses and employees and "the forum has endeavoured to reflect that in our recommendations".

The report recommended minimum wage rates for year one and two trainees remained at £10.50 and £11.75 per hour respectively for one more year from 1 April.

It also recommended an equivalent increase in the allowances available to employers for accommodation and meals provided to employees earning the main minimum wage rate, which Millar said she accepted.

The minister said: "The forum's report also reflected on the debate about a youth rate and possible changes to the way in which the formal trainee minimum wage policy is currently set.

"I will consider carefully the arguments that have emerged from the forum's consultation exercise, and in particular whether a further consultation on these aspects should take place."

articles.title: Lanny actor, 9, shares joy at getting lead role in Bristol Old Vic play
articles.summary: Atlas Johnson-Dutfield, from Bristol, shares the leading role with 10-year-old Lucian Thomas.
articles.body:
A nine-year-old who landed a leading role in a play with no professional acting experience says he "screamed the house down" when he found out.

Atlas Johnson-Dutfield from Bristol is sharing the role of Lanny with fellow youngster Lucian Thomas, 10, in the stage adaptation of Max Porter's acclaimed novel Lanny.

Atlas' mum Jada Johnson-Dutfield said she initially "felt sick" with nerves when watching him perform - but this was then overtaken by pride.

The young actor got the part following an open audition by the Bristol Old Vic theatre.

Atlas said he felt "super-duper happy" when he found out he had got the role.

"I shouted yes and fist pumped... dad was so confused and wondering why we were screaming," he added.

Based on the bestselling novel by Max Porter, Lanny has been adapted for the stage by West Country playwright Bea Roberts.

The play tells the story of Lanny and his family moving to a village near Bristol and awakening Dead Papa Toothwort, a mythic figure listening from the woods.

"Lanny is different from all the other kids and is connected to nature in a different way that other people can't see. He's different in a good way," Atlas said.

He added that he and Lucian, who share the part of Lanny, are now "like stage brothers".

Atlas' mother said her son had gone to acting classes after watching children in the Lion King stage show at the age of seven, at which point he asked if he could be in a play one day.

Describing the moment she first watched her son on stage himself, Johnson-Dutfield said: "When I first saw him up there it was just odd. I'll be honest I felt quite sick.

"I couldn't focus on the play. I was thinking 'I don't want this to go wrong'."

"After that I got over it, there was pride. I was just watching him in the whole process and seeing him grow," she added.

articles.title: Serbia’s students demand resignations in police, judiciary as they prepare to take power
articles.summary: Serbia’s student movement on Thursday demanded the resignations of top officials in the police, intelligence agencies and the judiciary as they prepare to take power after a historic election win last weekend against former strongman leader Aleksandar Vučić.
articles.body: BELGRADE, Serbia — Serbia’s student movement on Thursday demanded the resignations of top officials in the police, intelligence agencies and the judiciary as they prepare to take power after a historic election win last weekend against former strongman leader Aleksandar Vučić. The students at a news conference also urged Serbia’s election authorities to officially declare the final results of Sunday’s ballot without delay after a rerun at some 50 polling stations next Sunday, so that a new Parliament and government can be formed. The Students’ List movement swept the parliamentary election on Sunday against Vučić’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party, which has ruled unchallenged for 14 years. The outgoing authorities remain in control as the formal transition of power will take several weeks. “Changes are starting now,” student Filip Ubovic said at the news conference held at a central Belgrade park that used to be a sealed-off area occupied by Vučić’s loyalists. “Institutions belong to the citizens and the law applies to everyone.” Vučić’s party has gradually taken control over all state institutions since it came to power in 2012. The SNS party has been accused of rampant corruption and cronyism, links to organized crime and pressure on the judiciary, police and the media, which the populists have denied. The students on Thursday asked public servants to prevent outgoing officials from destroying documentation or evidence of potential wrongdoing. Vučić on Thursday held a news conference of his own, accusing the election winners of “revolutionary terror” after groups of people stormed the Informer TV station that led the preelection propaganda branding the students as traitors and enemies of the state. Suspicions of state corruption in infrastructure projects two years ago set off a wave of street protests after a collapsed canopy at a train station in Serbia’s north killed 16 people after a renovation. The students led those protests before challenging and defeating Vučić at the early ballot on Sunday. The students’ win on Sunday marks the first time that a grassroots youth movement toppled a well-established political leader. It comes at the moment when similar movements are mushrooming across Europe. The students said in their briefing that top police officials and the intelligence agencies had served Vučić’s party during the protests in violation of the law. They have been accused of using excessive force against protesters, illegal surveillance, detention and pressure on Vučić’s political opponents. The students also demanded changes in the judiciary and urgent investigations in top-level corruption cases that might have been sidelined due to political pressure under Vučić. They promised that all contracts and public spending deals will be reviewed. “The Students’ List is not here to take revenge,” Ubovic said. “We are not asking for political service but for the adherence to the laws, professionalism and responsibility.” There was no immediate response from the police commanders, judges and prosecutors whom the students asked to step down. The general manager of the state Serbian RTS television, Manja Grcic, has resigned while the public broadcaster’s branch in Novi Sad, the site of the November 2024 train station tragedy, has apologized to the viewers for selective and non-professional reporting. Serbia is formally seeking European Union membership but the bid has stalled under Vučić due to democratic backsliding and close ties to Russia. EU officials have offered help to the new authorities in boosting Serbia’s democracy and the rule of law.

articles.title: Offshore workers turn to weight-loss jabs to meet new helicopter weight limits
articles.summary: From Sunday anyone weighing more than 19st 7Ib (124kg) will be banned from flying to an offshore platform.
articles.body:
Hundreds of offshore workers have been using weight-loss jabs to help meet maximum weight rules for helicopter flights due to come into force next week.

From Sunday, anyone weighing more than 19st 7Ib (124kg) in civilian clothing and footwear will be banned from taking a flight to an offshore platform covered by UK safety regulations.

When the new rules were announced last year, about 2,200 workers were over the limit but that figure has now fallen to fewer than 250, according to Offshore Energies UK (OEUK).

The industry body told BBC Scotland News that on one platform, 60% of staff had been taking weight-loss drugs and extra fridge space had been provided to keep the medications cool.

The average weight of offshore workers has risen over recent decades, and increased by almost 1st 7Ib (10kg) since 2008.

The new weight limit policy came after the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) warned that rescue winches - which are critical during offshore emergencies - cannot safely lift heavier people.

The figure was decided upon after factoring in the weight of the rescuer, stretcher and other kit that would add to the combined total.

Hundreds of North Sea workers too heavy for new helicopter rules

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

OEUK health and safety manager Graham Skinner said a range of measures were being used to help offshore workers manage their weight, including gym equipment and healthier food options.

Alongside those, he said many had had chosen to make use of the latest medical advances in controlling appetite and digestion.

"What we know is that offshore workers are using weight-loss jabs regardless of the policies. Last year we saw in some cases 60% of workers turning up with weight-loss jabs," he told BBC Scotland News.

"That's brought our average weight down in a very short space of time. I think that's very common in society and it can potentially be a really useful tool if somebody's got a lot of weight to lose it can get them in a good place."

He said initially staff appeared to be funding the medication themselves, although he thought it possible that some firms were now supporting them with the costs.

The weight-limit policy has been criticised by the RMT union which claimed there had been a lack of consultation, and that it could lead to experienced staff being excluded from offshore operations.

Earlier this year, BBC Scotland spoke to one occupational health expert in Aberdeen who said some clients were "really stressed" by the new rules while others had chosen to leave the industry.

Companies could offer staff alternative onshore roles but Skinner warned: "If somebody has chosen not to lose weight then there's a real possibility they could lose their job."

He said there were a number of safety reasons for having weight-limit controls such as working in confined spaces or ability to quickly exit a helicopter - but the actual numbers had been driven by the lifting capacity of the winches.

"It's the same winch on all search and rescue helicopters and if somebody needs to be rescued due to a health or safety incident the winch has limitations and we can't allow people to exceed those," he said.

Workers will be asked to declare if they are under the weight limit and this will be checked at the heliport.

He said employers in the industry had been working "really hard" to ensure as many staff as possible complied with the new rules and he hoped the number of staff over the weight limit could be reduced still further.

articles.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand options for customers
articles.summary: Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, compared to the 100,000 currently available on the platform, the firms said.
articles.body:
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.

DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.

Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.

"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.

"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.

For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.

He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".

The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.

Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.

"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.

In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.

DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.

The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.

New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."

"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

articles.title: In 2016, an Indianapolis flower charity began with $9,000 raised in 45 minutes and its first hospital delivery, ten years later it has reportedly reached 175,000 bouquets for patients across the city
articles.summary: An Indianapolis non-profit group that reuses donated flowers for hospital patients marked its tenth anniversary on 27 October 2026.
articles.body: An Indianapolis non-profit group that reuses donated flowers for hospital patients marked its tenth anniversary on 27 October 2026. It delivered its 175,000th flower arrangement at Eskenazi Health. Random Acts of Flowers Indianapolis (RAFI) reached the milestone ten years after it began local work in 2016. The charity got started after a burst of giving, when supporters donated $9,000 within 45 minutes to open a branch in the city. This allowed its first hospital deliveries later that year. The group depends on volunteers who collect unwanted flowers from weddings, memorial services, florists, and grocery stores. Teams arrange the stems into fresh displays. They then deliver them to patients in healthcare facilities, nursing homes, and hospices across the Indianapolis area. The organisation said the milestone delivery stands for thousands of personal moments. They aim to give emotional support to people facing illness, loneliness, or long hospital stays.Milestone delivery at Eskenazi HealthThe 175,000th bouquet was given out during a special anniversary visit to patients at Eskenazi Health. It is one of the main medical centres the charity has served since it began. According to a report from Indianapolis radio station 93.1 WIBC, the event showed the steady community support that has kept the volunteer network running for ten years. Kelly McBride, Executive Director of Random Acts of Flowers Indianapolis, stressed that the real value of the milestone lies in the personal connections made at patients’ bedsides over the past decade. “Ten years and 175,000 bouquets delivered. That is 175,000 moments of kindness and joy we have shared,” Kelly McBride said in a statement reported by WIBC. Kelly McBride added that each arrangement relies on many people in the community. She said “each RAFI arrangement begins with donated flowers and is made possible through the collective efforts of volunteers, floral donors, community partners and supporters.”Origin of the flower recycling modelThe idea behind Random Acts of Flowers began in 2007. That year, founder Larsen Jay survived a serious accident and was stuck in bed in a hospital intensive care unit. While he recovered, Larsen Jay saw that his room was full of flowers sent by well-wishers. Many patients near him got none. He saw how uplifting the flowers were, so he began moving his extra flowers to other hospital rooms. This led to the creation of a national non-profit group. The Indianapolis chapter was set up in 2016 after local organisers raised $9,000 in just 45 minutes for seed money. This first push let the local group open a workshop, find volunteer florists, and set up delivery partnerships with hospitals in central Indiana. Over the past ten years, the Indianapolis group has grown to handle tens of thousands of donated stems each year. It keeps flowers from going to waste while serving healthcare networks across the region.Volunteer logistics and community partnershipsThe daily work of Random Acts of Flowers Indianapolis relies on a well-organised volunteer system that runs out of a local workshop. Volunteers drive to partner sites, including florists, event planners, and funeral homes. They pick up unsold or extra flowers that would otherwise end up in landfills. At the workshop, volunteer arrangers trim, freshen, and put the stems into small, portable vases. Delivery teams then bring the finished arrangements by hand to patient rooms. Staff at the hospitals and other facilities work with the charity to make sure the bouquets reach people who have few visitors or who are going through long medical treatment. The charity confirmed through WIBC that it plans to keep its regular delivery schedules to healthcare facilities in the Indianapolis area. articles.title: A rock formation collapse in Turkey’s touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 3
articles.summary: Parts of a large volcanic rock formation crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia on Thursday, killing at least three people and injuring five others, officials said.
articles.body: Parts of a large volcanic rock formation crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia on Thursday, killing at least three people and injuring five others, officials said. A section of the rock formation — known as a fairy chimney — tumbled in Cappadocia’s Goreme region, prompting authorities to deploy medical and rescue teams. Gov. Huseyin Kok said recent heavy rains likely caused the collapse, which occurred near a parking lot at an entrance to the site. He said rescue teams were continuing to search for other people who may be trapped under the debris. “We hope that there are no other casualties,” the governor said. “We are deeply saddened.” Kok said two of the three dead were Turkish nationals. He did not provide information on the third victim. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation was launched into the incident. HaberTurk news channel showed heavy machinery removing chunks of rock from the foot of the formation. Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is a UNESCO World Heritage-listed site famed for its distinctive rock formations and ancient underground cities. It is one of the country’s most visited tourism locations. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day holiday, when the area would have been crowded with visitors.

articles.title: In 1980, a Texas man called his stepson his child in a will; after the man died in 2020, the stepson battled surviving relatives over inheritance, but a jury found there had been no legal or informal adoption
articles.summary: In 1980, a Texas man drafted a will that referred to his stepson as “my child,” language that would later become the centre of a bitter family inheritance
articles.body: In 1980, a Texas man drafted a will that referred to his stepson as “my child,” language that would later become the centre of a bitter family inheritance dispute. More than four decades after the will was signed, and after the man died in 2020, his stepson argued that he had been informally adopted and was therefore entitled to inherit under the document. Surviving relatives disagreed, insisting that affection, support, and familiar words in a will did not amount to a legal adoption. A Harris County jury ultimately agreed with the relatives, finding that no legal or informal adoption had taken place. The case, Maniscalco v. Womack, was recently reviewed by Texas’ First Court of Appeals, which affirmed the judgment against the stepson’s claim. It is also documented by Justia Law, and details from it are shared below.The dispute began long before the courtroom fight. Huland Eugene “Gene” Womack married Norma Womack in 1970. Norma brought two sons from an earlier marriage into the household: Jack Maniscalco and Tommy Maniscalco. Jack was not quite nine years old when Gene and Norma married, meaning Gene became a constant adult presence during much of Jack’s childhood. According to evidence described in the appellate case summary, Gene helped support the boys and took part in their upbringing, and Norma later testified that Gene had agreed to adopt them.In 1980, Gene executed a will leaving his estate to Norma. The will also contained an important contingency: if Norma died before him, his estate would pass to “my child, JACK MADISON MANISCALCO, JR. and any other child or children legally adopted by me,” as per Justia Law. An addendum to the will likewise described Jack as Gene’s son and addressed Gene’s expectations for Jack and Tommy’s care. To anyone reading those documents without knowing the family history, the language could easily suggest that Jack was Gene’s legally recognised child.But the relationship between Gene and Norma did not last. They separated in 1987 and divorced in 1992, as per Justia Law. In their divorce pleadings, the couple stated that no children had been born to or adopted during the marriage. Gene never filed a formal adoption proceeding for Jack, and the parental rights of Jack’s biological father were never terminated. Those facts would become central when the estate dispute reached court, because Texas law draws a clear distinction between a stepparent who acts like a parent and one who has legally adopted a child.What happened after Gene diedGene died in 2020. At first, one of his brothers claimed that Gene had died without a valid will, which would have meant his estate would pass under Texas intestacy rules rather than according to the 1980 document. Jack responded by offering Gene’s will for probate and asserting that Gene had adopted him by estoppel, sometimes called equitable adoption. In practical terms, Jack argued that even if the adoption was never completed through formal legal proceedings, Gene’s conduct and promises should prevent his relatives from denying Jack the status of an adopted child.The case became a four-day jury trial. Family members, friends, and other witnesses testified about Gene’s relationship with Jack and whether Gene had truly agreed to adopt him. Jack and Norma described a longstanding parent-child bond. They said Gene supported Jack, participated in his activities, and referred to him as a son. The will itself, with its reference to Jack as Gene’s child, was also part of the evidence supporting Jack’s position.The jury, however, was not persuaded that those facts established an adoption. It held that Gene had not adopted Jack, either under the law or under the equitable doctrine on which Jack relied. The jury also found that Jack, Darren Womack and Richard Womack acted in good faith and with just cause in pursuing their respective claims, awarding attorneys’ fees. Thus, Jack’s emotional and familial ties to Gene did not translate into a right to inherit under the will.Why the language of the will was inadequateThe legal question wasn’t whether Gene loved Jack or whether Jack saw Gene as a father figure. The issue was whether Gene had made an enforceable agreement to adopt Jack and whether the circumstances warranted treating the adoption as complete without formal legal action. Texas law requires more than a close stepparent relationship or the informal use of parental terms. A claimant must prove the elements needed for equitable adoption, including an enforceable or equitable basis for treating the decedent as having agreed to adopt the claimant.That distinction matters because wills are legal instruments, but they do not automatically perform every function people may assume they do. Calling someone “my child” in a will can express affection, intended beneficiaries, or a personal understanding of family. It does not necessarily create an adoption, especially where the person writing the will had never adopted the child, never terminated the biological parent’s rights, and had earlier stated in divorce filings that no children had been adopted during the marriage.The appellate court treated the question as fact-intensive. It considered the testimony about Gene’s role in Jack’s life, the wording of the will, the absence of an adoption proceeding, and the divorce record. In the end, the First Court of Appeals affirmed the probate court’s judgment. The jury’s rejection of Jack’s adoption-by-estoppel claim remained intact, as did the lower court’s rulings on jury argument, evidence, a requested mistrial, and attorneys’ fees.A family dispute with a legal lessonThe case is a reminder that family relationships can be real and meaningful without being legally formalised. Gene may have been a father in every practical sense to Jack during his childhood. He may have supported him, helped raise him, and used the language of parenthood in his will. Yet the jury found that those facts did not prove the legal agreement and performance necessary for an equitable adoption under Texas law.For families in blended households, the lesson is uncomfortable but important. If a stepparent intends for a stepchild to inherit as a child, the safest course is to make that intention legally explicit. That may mean completing an adoption where appropriate, clearly identifying the stepchild as a named beneficiary in the will, or using precise estate-planning language that does not depend on an assumption about legal parentage. A vague reference to “my child” may carry deep emotional meaning, but it may not survive a challenge from other relatives after death.The appellate court also addressed costs arising from the appeal. It ordered Jack to pay 60 percent of the clerk’s-record costs, while the remaining 40 percent was assessed jointly and severally among Jack, Darren Womack, and Richard Womack. The court explained that Texas Rule of Appellate Procedure 34.5 allows costs to be allocated when a party requests unnecessary materials for the record, regardless of who ultimately prevails in the broader appeal.More than forty years after Gene Womack wrote the words “my child” in his will, a jury decided that those words did not make Jack his legal child. The ruling does not erase the relationship the two men may have shared, but it shows how sharply Texas law separates family bonds from formal adoption and inheritance rights. For anyone relying on informal family understandings in estate planning, the case is a cautionary example of why clarity in legal documents can matter as much as love and intention.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1600, William Gilbert argued that Earth was a giant magnet and coined the language of electricity; his book passed through a historic library and several auctions before selling for Rs 58.5 lakh in 2026
articles.summary: Published in 1600, William Gilbert’s De Magnete argued that Earth itself behaved like a giant magnet.
articles.body: Published in 1600, William Gilbert’s De Magnete argued that Earth itself behaved like a giant magnet. Four centuries after it challenged conventional ideas about the natural world, the book helped lay the foundations of modern electrical science. Written by English physician and natural philosopher William Gilbert, the book also introduced important terminology for understanding electrical phenomena.The first edition of the book is attracting attention once again at an auction conducted by Christie's. The book was sold for $61,440, approximately Rs 58.5 lakh. The copy, offered as Lot 61 in the auction house's Fine Printed Books, Manuscripts, and Science sale in New York on October 13, 2026, had been estimated at 25,000–35,000.The physician who saw Earth as a giant magnetWilliam Gilbert was born in 1544 and studied at Cambridge. He was an English physician who became one of the most influential early investigators of magnetism. He also practised medicine in London and eventually served as physician to Queen Elizabeth I.During Gilbert's lifetime, magnets were familiar objects, particularly because of their use in compasses. However, many explanations of magnetic behaviour remained rooted in inherited ideas rather than systematic experimentation.Gilbert sought to investigate these phenomena through observation and practical experiments. His findings culminated in De Magnete, Magneticisque Corporibus, et de Magno Magnete Tellure, a Latin title that can be understood as a treatise on magnets, magnetic bodies and Earth, the great magnet.The book was published in London by Peter Short in 1600. It was then known as the first major English scientific treatise to rely on experimental methods of research. It brought together observations, demonstrations and explanations in an attempt to establish a coherent account of magnetism.Gilbert's central argument was incredible: Earth was not merely a place on which magnetic phenomena occurred; it was itself a vast magnet.How he supported the theoryTo support his theory, Gilbert used a spherical magnet, often referred to as a terrella, meaning a little Earth. By studying how a compass needle behaved around this model, he could investigate magnetic direction on a small scale and compare it with the behaviour observed on the planet.How De Magnete helped lay the foundations of electrical scienceThe ancient Greeks had observed that amber could attract lightweight objects after being rubbed. Gilbert explored this effect and distinguished it from magnetic attraction, helping establish that the two phenomena required separate explanations.He used the Latin word electricus, associated with amber, to describe materials that displayed this kind of attraction. His work helped introduce the vocabulary of electricity, including the terms “electric force” and “electric attraction”, as noted in the historical references cited by Christie's.Gilbert also developed the versorium, an early instrument used to detect electrical effects. These experiments were significant because they reflected a change in how natural phenomena were studied. Instead of relying solely on the authority of earlier writers, Gilbert argued through observation and repeatable demonstrations. His book provided enough detail about many experiments for other investigators to attempt them.From a historic library to the auction roomAccording to Christie's catalogue, the volume was once part of the Signet Library, a historic legal library in Edinburgh, Scotland. Its eighteenth-century calf binding bears the library's arms. The copy was subsequently sold by Sotheby's on April 11, 1960, as Lot 1189.The book later appeared at Christie's New York on December 14, 2014, as Lot 221. It was acquired at that auction by its present owner, identified in the 2026 catalogue as a California collector. The volume was then offered again in the October 2026 sale.The 2026 copy was described as a folio volume measuring approximately 28.2 by 18.4 centimetres. Its features include a woodcut printer's device on the title page, numerous illustrations within the text, a large folding woodcut diagram and decorative initials.Why a 426-year-old book still mattersWhen De Magnete appeared in 1600, the systematic study of electricity was still in its infancy. There were no electric power grids, household electrical appliances or modern electronic devices. His assertion that Earth was a giant magnet was an important step towards understanding terrestrial magnetism. His investigations of amber and electrical attraction helped establish a vocabulary and experimental approach that later researchers could build upon.The book's sale for $61,440 in October 2026, equivalent to roughly Rs 58.5 lakh, therefore represents more than the market value of an old volume.And that’s why even after four centuries, the book continues to attract people.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Operation Ghostbusters': DOJ unveils crackdown on student aid fraud scheme
articles.summary: The Department of Justice announced a sprawling effort to crack down on a student aid fraud scheme involving fake identities and "ghost students."
articles.body:
The Department of Justice announced a sprawling operation seeking to end an elaborate student aid fraud scheme that authorities say has bilked potentially hundreds of millions of dollars from taxpayers.

The effort, dubbed "Operation Ghostbusters ," aims to crack down on an international fraud scam that has funneled stolen federal student aid dollars into offshore accounts since at least 2021.

At an Oct. 29 news conference, Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald described the scheme, detailing how suspects steal Americans' identities before applying to universities, receiving federal student aid and running off with the money.

McDonald said perpetrators are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create so-called "ghost students," filling out college applications and even completing coursework. Some fraudsters go as far as creating "the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present," he said.

"These are not isolated errors. This is organized fraud at scale," McDonald said, adding that taxpayer losses could potentially reach "several hundred million dollars."

In California alone, one-third of community college applications submitted in 2024 were reportedly flagged as fraudulent, McDonald said. Heith Janke, assistant director of the FBI's criminal division, said the agency has so far identified more than $32 million in losses, with millions more suspected, in similar student aid schemes.

"This stops now," Janke said in a statement. "The FBI, working hand-in-hand with our partners at the Department of Education and Department of Justice will follow all evidence, track every dollar, and pursue each criminal who seeks to exploit our nation's systems."

The government's expansive investigation involves 26 FBI field offices and more than 20 U.S. attorney's offices, according to the DOJ. There are at least 40 open cases related to the scam.

McDonald said the operation, which began in April, has so far led to charges against five people and the seizure of more than $750,000 in crypto currency tied to networks in Kenya. The defendants have been indicted in multiple states, including Nebraska and New Jersey.

McDonald said the first round of charges is "just the beginning."

"If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build their future, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.

This story has been updated to add new information.

Christopher Cann is a national correspondent for USA TODAY. Contact him via email at ccann@usatoday.com.

articles.title: UAE sentences eight people to life over arms supplies to Sudan’s army
articles.summary: Defendants handed ⁠life sentences amid tensions between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi over Sudan’s war and the RSF.
articles.body:
A court in the United Arab Emirates has sentenced eight people to ⁠life imprisonment over ⁠arms trafficking and money laundering to Sudan’s army, state media report.

The individuals supplied weapons and military equipment to the Sudanese army and were part of a money-laundering network connecting the two countries, the Emirati state-run news agency WAM said on Thursday.

It said the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal concluded on Thursday that the convicted individuals had participated in an integrated scheme for the illicit trafficking of weapons, ammunition and military equipment.

The accused were also found to have forged documents using companies and bank accounts in the UAE to channel funds relating to the arms deals and “conceal” their sources and destinations.

The court ordered the confiscation of ammunition and communications devices used in the crimes and the deportation of those convicted from the UAE after serving their sentences, WAM reported.

The “arms deals, money laundering endangered UAE interests”, the court order said.

Ties between the UAE and ⁠Sudan have deteriorated ⁠as the Sudanese military has accused Abu Dhabi of supplying arms ⁠to its rival in Sudan’s civil war, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, which it has been fighting ‌since April 2023. The UAE has denied ‌the ‌allegation.

The war has displaced more than 14 million people and created severe poverty and food shortages.

This week, more than 100 people – mostly women and children – were killed when military drones hit a busy city market frequented by RSF fighters in the city of Nyala in the western region of Darfur.

Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said a second attack hit a civilian neighbourhood. MSF said a hospital it supports in Nyala received 36 bodies in the hours after that attack, 21 of them wearing civilian clothing, and its teams saw more than 150 wounded in the emergency room.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has previously accused the RSF of carrying out war crimes and a possible crime against humanity in its takeover of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur state, after forcing Sudan’s army to withdraw from its last stronghold in the Darfur region.

articles.title: Spanish train crash yet another blow to Sánchez’s government ahead of elections in November
articles.summary: The deadly train crash in Spain’s Toledo province has sparked fresh criticism of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s government and raised questions about the country’s investment in public infrastructure – just weeks before national elections in November.
articles.body: The deadly train crash in Spain’s Toledo province has sparked fresh criticism of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s government and raised questions about the country’s investment in public infrastructure – just weeks before national elections in November. Wednesday’s crash marks the third deadly train disaster in Spain this year, thrusting worries about railway maintenance, investment and staffing levels into the spotlight. The tragedy deals a fresh blow to Sánchez’ left-wing government, which has already faced corruption scandals, protests over housing affordability and the Ceuta mass migrant crossing earlier this year. Sánchez took a gamble by calling a snap election for November 29, and although his Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) is polling behind the conservative People’s Party (PP), it had been gaining ground in recent weeks. But this latest catastrophe could clip the wings of any comeback. “On top of a crisis of confidence in Sánchez, you also have a crisis of confidence in the railway institution,” said analyst Grégoire Roos, the director of the Europe program at Chatham House. He said while the train disaster is unlikely to be the tipping point of an election in which Sánchez is already polling behind, it could fuel right-wing opposition parties. “It’s undeniable that this will further hinder public confidence,” Roos told CNN. “An environment of such distrust can only play in favor of (far-right party) Vox, and to some extent to the (conservative) Partido Popular.” Spain’s Transportation Minister Óscar Puente said the collision, which killed at least 69 people and injured scores more, was caused by both computer system failure and apparent human error. That sparked an immediate backlash from unions, which stressed the need for a full investigation, and that one train controller should not be used as a scapegoat for wider systemic problems. Protesters and far right groups gathered on Wednesday night in the Spanish capital Madrid to demand Puente’s resignation and a change in government. Videos from the demonstrations showed some protesters holding signs saying “corruption kills” and “leave!” next to pictures of the Spanish prime minister. Sánchez has responded to the crash by saying that his government is working to “clarify every last detail of this tragedy and of course to reinforce security so that this does not happen again.” From the scene of the crash in the immediate aftermath on Wednesday, he expressed his “full solidarity” with victims’ families and said that “if there has been negligence, it will come to light. And if there have been failures in the safety system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness.” Sánchez added that “it’s clear that we have suffered two terrible tragedies involving high-speed rail in the same year,” acknowledging the other major crash in January in Córdoba province, which killed more than 40 people on the same line. “We will rebuild trust in our high-speed system,” Sánchez said. Strong backlash from unions Transportation Minister Puente publicly stated that Wednesday’s crash was the result of a computer system failure that led to an issue with the LZB train management safety system along a 40-mile stretch of track, causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically. At that point, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, ADIF, took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow a high-speed train to continue despite a red light, Puente said, which ultimately resulted in its collision with a stationary train. Unions immediately balked at that explanation, though, and demanded that “all the circumstances that led to this tragedy are investigated.” “We do not accept that the actions of one single worker are placed under the microscope while the managerial decision and corporate policies are relegated to the background,” the railway workers’ union UGT said, adding that issues of staffing shortages, excessive workloads, poor organization and outdated equipment that “should equally be scrutinized.” Spain’s train drivers held a pre-planned nationwide strike Thursday to call for stronger safety measures. The train drivers’ union SEMAF criticized how audio from the control center at Madrid’s Atocha station had been leaked to Spanish media in the wake of the crash, with spokesperson Teo Moreno telling CNN the recordings only gave “half the picture.” “Leaking those audios was regrettable, and it’s the same people who failed to do the right investment who are leaking the audios to scapegoat one single worker,” he said. Another union representing civil servants, CSIF, said in a statement that it demands the government “respect the investigation and the presumption of innocence for the head of traffic at ADIF.” The trade union accused Puente of pointing the finger at “hardworking person” instead of “assuming his responsibilities.” The civil servants’ union said it had also warned in September of “excess hours” for the working days of ADIF staff. CNN has reached out to the Spanish transport ministry and ADIF for comment. Spain’s rail traffic controllers’ union, SCF, is also urging the government to invest more in the railway safety system and accelerate its replacement with more modern technology. Spain’s transportation ministry is working to upgrade the current LZB safety system, which was introduced in 1992 and has already been phased out in other parts of the country. The ministry has previously announced hundreds of millions of euros of investments into modernizing the high-speed rail network, including this particular section running from Madrid to Seville. Like the other unions, SCF has also argued there are pervasive issues with long working hours and inadequate staffing at train station control centers. “The rail operator, ADIF, has not made plans for a generational change in the workforce, so you have a generation of old controllers who are retiring, and they have not been replaced,” union spokeswoman Raquel Ayllón told CNN in the aftermath of the disaster. “In some instances, our controllers cannot take toilet breaks because there’s nobody on staff to take over from them,” Ayllón said. “It’s clear that if you want to have three trains departing from the station every minute, a single person cannot handle that level of traffic.” The union spokeswoman noted that after the previous train disaster in Córdoba province, the rail operator opened a new training center, but those new recruits won’t join the workforce until next year. She also highlighted issues with inadequate training and experience among staff. “Years ago, in order to work in a busy station like Atocha – Madrid’s busiest – you’d have to have ten years’ experience at least. Now, they just bring people in from the first year,” Ayllón said. Investment in new rail lines rather than maintenance Spain has rapidly expanded its rail network over the last decade. According to a European Union report based on the most recent statistics from 2024, Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in the EU. Between 2018 and 2022, that network grew by nearly 1,000 km (570 miles). However, the EU report notes that most funds for the rail infrastructure were allocated to new lines, “whereas upgrades and renewals played a minor role.” Spanish journalist and political analyst Ramón González Férriz said the country invested a lot of money into infrastructure before the 2008 financial crisis – and the railways became both a sign of modernization and a point of pride for Spaniards. But the large railway system, along with other infrastructure like an extensive network of regional airports, became very expensive to maintain for successive governments, he told CNN. “This government increased the spending on pensions – that is the big elephant in the room,” González Férriz said, also noting rises in spending due to the pandemic and inflation pressures. “You can think it’s okay, or it isn’t – but the fact is that we began spending a lot of money on a lot of things that were not the infrastructure.” In the years since, public sentiment about the country’s infrastructure and public services has tanked. He said the successive train disasters and lack of confidence in public services are unlikely to push left-wing voters to switch to the right, but it could increase the number of people who decide to stay home on election day. “The government was making a campaign based on optimism and hope, and that Spain is growing when most of Europe is not growing… and the president is young and handsome and likes pop music… But now it’s impossible,” González Férriz added. CNN’s Pau Mosquera, Duarte Mendonca, Billy Stockwell, Caitlin Danaher and Sophie Tanno contributed to this report.

articles.title: Facing drought, Texas cotton farmers drilled by their hog pen in 1918; the well struck 2,500 barrels a day, and investors sold the stake for $1.8 million
articles.summary: In 1918, Texas farmers Shields and Cassie Fowler transformed their drought-stricken cotton farm into a lucrative oil venture, discovering a well with a potential of 2,500 barrels a day, which later sold for $1.8 million.
articles.body: Drought threatened the livelihoods of cotton farmers Shields and Cassie Fowler in the summer of 1918. The pair were considering leaving their farm near Burkburnett in Wichita County, Texas; instead, they decided to explore for oil after they learned about earlier discoveries in the surrounding area. The Fowlers gathered financial and material support from their relatives, neighbours and local businesses, and began drilling near their hog pen. The well, known as Fowler No. 1, struck oil in late July at a depth of approximately 1,735 feet, with a reported flowing potential of 2,500 barrels a day. The discovery helped launch the Burkburnett Townsite oil boom. Eventually, as reported by the Texas State Historical Association (TSHA), the investors in Fowler Farm Oil Company sold their interests to Magnolia Petroleum Company for $1.8 million in cash.From a drought-stricken farm to an oil prospectThe Fowlers’ decision came as oil exploration was already reportedly expanding across Wichita County. Near Electra in 1911, the county’s first commercial oil discovery was recorded. This was followed by further discoveries around Burkburnett in 1912. These discoveries showed that oil could be found beneath North Texas farmland. However, drilling remained financially risky as investors could spend a fortune on a well without finding commercially productive oil. Meanwhile, for the Fowlers, the drought threatened their agricultural livelihood; thus, the nearby discoveries offered a reason to try an alternative.S.L. Fowler persuaded friends, neighbours and local businesses to help finance a well on his farm. According to the TSHA, contributors invested between $100 and $500 each or supplied materials needed for the project. Their neighbour Walter Cline, who owned three drilling rigs, agreed to provide a rig and crew in exchange for a $1,000 interest. As Fowler lacked structural space on his operational land, the crew set up the rig and began drilling directly alongside his hog pen. The participants planned to form Fowler Farm Oil Company if the well proved productive.Though the exact date of the discovery varies among historical accounts, the sources agree that the well struck oil in late July. It reportedly reached a depth of about 1,735 feet in the Cisco sands and had an alleged potential of 2,500 barrels a day.A discovery that accelerated the Burkburnett oil boomThe Fowler well prompted a rush to secure drilling sites in Burkburnett. By late August 1918, around three weeks following the discovery, 56 rigs were drilling in the town, as noted by the TSHA. With the rise in crude prices, the surge was further fueled. Additionally, lease prices rose as landowners and investors competed for promising sites, with some town-lot leases reaching $1,000.The Fowler discovery could be looked at as part of a broader expansion in the county’s oil industry, rather than the beginning of oil exploration there. Initially, many wells in the developing field flowed between 100 and 500 barrels a day, while some produced 1,000 to 3,000 barrels daily. To support transport of the increasing volume of crude, the Texas Company laid a four-inch pipeline with a capacity of approximately 5,000 to 6,000 barrels a day.Notably, for the investors in Fowler Farm Oil Company, the discovery brought a substantial financial return. The TSHA documents mention that they sold their interests to Magnolia Petroleum for $1.8 million in cash. The figure refers to the investors’ interest in the venture. Nevertheless, the transaction underscores the value that a successful discovery could command during the early stages of the Burkburnett boom.By the end of 1918, Wichita County’s annual crude production had exceeded around 11.5 million barrels, as noted by TSHA. The local demand for housing, supplies, transport and other services also increased with the influx of drilling crews, investors and businesses. Therefore, the Fowler discovery could be seen as the one that opened the way for this transition, although later discoveries, especially in 1919 and 1920, contributed further to the region’s petroleum development.You use AI every day. articles.title: Machado pushes for new elections in first news conference since returning to Venezuela
articles.summary: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado said she returned to the country from exile this past week to mobilize society as she pushes for new elections next year.
articles.body: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado said she returned to the country from exile this past week to mobilize society as she pushes for new elections next year. “I have returned to finish a task and to fulfill a mandate,” she said Thursday in her first news conference since her return. The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate thanked the US government for leading a democratic transition process in the South American country, saying Secretary of State Marco Rubio has outlined a sequence of events that includes holding presidential elections in 2027. “This addresses a national urgency with a sense of responsibility. It has also made clear — based on what has transpired in recent days — that the democratic transition is irreversible,” she said. Neither the United States nor the Venezuelan government have set a date for new elections. Rubio said on Monday that Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure needs to be changed in order to hold a valid election. A senior State Department official said they expect Venezuela to have a new Supreme Tribunal of Justice in place by the end of year and a new National Electoral Council (CNE) shortly thereafter. Once those institutions are replaced, Venezuela’s acting leader will have to declare a permanent vacancy in the presidency, which will trigger a six-month period for new elections, the State Department official said. The CNE will then determine a date of that election. Impact of return Machado returned on Sunday to crowds of cheering supporters, whom she said all demanded a free Venezuela. “I heard only one word, the same one: freedom,” she said Thursday. Machado left in December for Norway to accept the Nobel Peace Prize, which she was awarded for promoting democratic rights in her country. A month after she left, the United States toppled and captured her rival, strongman leader Nicolas Maduro, in a military operation on January 3. “Thanks to the actions of the United States government, Maduro is facing justice, and the floodgates of freedom have been opened,” Machado said Thursday. Within days of Maduro’s ouster, Washington began working with his successor, acting President Delcy Rodríguez, to enact political reforms and steer the nation toward a democratic transition. Rodriguez has so far met just about every demand from the US, including releasing hundreds of political prisoners, allowing some exiles to return home and making it easier for US companies to invest in the country. The US has also brokered reconciliation talks between the acting government and several high-profile opposition figures such as Dinorah Figuera. Machado reiterated on Thursday that she is not part of those talks but said she hopes they succeed. Shortly before Machado’s speech, Rodríguez also addressed the nation. She did not directly acknowledge Machado’s return, but addressed her detractors in the recorded message, saying: “To those who think differently from me, I do not ask you to change your opinion. I ask you to judge by the facts. Less fighting, more solutions.” Regarding the electoral calendar in the South American country — an open question since Maduro’s capture — Rodríguez reiterated that “there will be elections, as mandated by our Constitution.” “The election should not be a problem or make us go back to times of confrontation that no one wants anymore,” she urged. She also announced the continuation of reforms, including a promise that no one would be detained without judicial warrants, a long held demand from human rights groups. Rodríguez also revealed that the government is assessing whether non-essential assets currently held by the government will be offered to the private sector, or to former owners. The acting president said the process is “already well underway. Private property is a protected right guaranteed by our Constitution.” Machado welcomed Rodríguez’s comments, saying her commitment to new elections means the government is feeling the impact of her return. Asked if there are plans to meet with the acting president, Machado said, “No, I have not received any message from the United States or from Ms. Rodríguez.” Sidelined opposition Washington has so far sidelined Machado from the political transition process despite having a friendly relationship with the opposition leader. In January, Machado gifted US President Donald Trump her Nobel Prize, hoping the gesture would nudge him toward supporting her fight to become Venezuela’s next leader. Trump accepted the gift without endorsing her. He had previously called her a “very nice woman” but claimed she “does not have the support or the respect within the country” to lead it. Still, Machado has continued to back the Trump administration while simultaneously condemning the acting Venezuelan government that it’s been working with, which she considers a continuation of the repressive Maduro regime. During her 10 months in exile, Machado repeatedly vowed to return home and hinted that she would run for president if an election were held. She had attempted to re-enter Venezuela several times over the past few months without success, saying she was impeded by the acting government. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday the US had spoken with the interim Venezuelan authorities about Machado’s return and claimed that any “impediments” to her arrival “had nothing to do with us.” Machado didn’t provide details about how she returned, but said she received help from many people both inside and outside the country, including what she described as an “exceptionally well-qualified” team. Machado added that she had learned from her previous failed attempts to enter the country and did things differently. “And let me tell you: They didn’t see it coming,” she said of the acting government.

articles.title: Albanian opposition storms parliament, sets off flares and smoke bombs
articles.summary: Opposition lawmakers disrupt parliament session, accusing prime minister of downplaying ongoing antigovernment protests.
articles.body:
The leader of Albania’s opposition has branded members of the government as “criminals”, while he and fellow lawmakers disrupted a parliamentary session by setting off flares and smoke bombs.

Sali Berisha and other opposition members stormed parliament in the capital, Tirana, on Thursday in support of demonstrators , who are demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation. Berisha and his colleagues unsuccessfully tried to prevent a vote on a new law governing the country’s central bank.

“These [ruling lawmakers] are criminals and ⁠they deserve tear gas, rubber bullets, cracked skulls and broken bones, not the young people,” Berisha, leader of the Democratic Party of Albania, said.

The protests began in May and were triggered by Rama’s preliminary approval of a luxury resort linked to Jared Kushner , the son-in-law of United States President Donald Trump.

The student-led protest movement has since evolved into something far bigger, with demonstrators citing economic stagnation, alleged corruption and poor education standards, coupled with high tuition fees.

The anti-government protests are Albania’s largest in decades and have turned violent, injuring hundreds of people, including police officers. Government buildings, banks and private buildings have also been attacked and set on fire.

Rama has been in office for 13 years and has refused to resign after winning a fourth term last year.

As Berisha addressed parliament on Thursday, his colleagues surrounded him while holding photos of protesters allegedly injured by rubber bullets.

Rama has introduced fines of more than $6,000 for anyone who attends a protest that turns violent, even if they did not participate in such acts. That is six times Albania’s average monthly salary of around $1,000.

Rama has announced a series of measures aimed at easing the protests. These include increasing the monthly scholarship stipend for students from low-income families, according to Albania’s public broadcaster, Radio Televizioni Shqiptar. Scholarships have also been extended to master’s degree students. Rama has also announced subsidised rent for students, the broadcaster reported.

articles.title: Al Jazeera marks 30th anniversary with network overhaul
articles.summary: Marking three decades, Al Jazeera unveils a new structure: three channels, 33 programmes, and tech-driven innovation.
articles.body:
Al Jazeera is marking its 30-year anniversary with a transformation of the network, introducing a three-channel structure for its Arabic-language broadcasting operation and 33 programmes aimed at providing audiences with more in-depth coverage and analysis.

Since its launch on November 1, 1996 , the Qatar-based network has helped reshape Arab journalism, challenging dominant political narratives and providing a platform for political debate rarely seen on television in the region at the time.

Reflecting on this enduring legacy during a special anniversary episode of the network’s Arabic-language Baad al-Bath podcast, veteran anchor Khadija Benguenna detailed the foundational shifts the network brought to the Arab news industry.

Benguenna said that Al Jazeera had popularised practices such as breaking news alerts, continuous live coverage, and exclusive reporting, which were subsequently adopted by other Arab broadcasters.

Former Al Jazeera news director Ahmad al-Sheikh echoed that sentiment during his appearance on the same broadcast. He described the Arab world’s media environment as previously devoid of independent voices, and credited Al Jazeera with providing an example for other Arab broadcasters to improve standards across the board.

The anniversary brings a significant restructuring of the Al Jazeera Media Network’s Arabic-language news services, separating rolling breaking news coverage, live event broadcasting, and more in-depth reporting across three channels.

Speaking to the Qatari newspaper Al Raya , Asef Hamidi, the managing director of Al Jazeera Arabic, described the changes as a “new renaissance” for Al Jazeera. “We are talking about numerous paths undergoing significant development that the audience will notice,” Hamidi said.

Hamidi, who was appointed to his current position in September 2025, said the restructuring was intended to address the growing volume and complexity of news and the need to offer audiences different ways of following events.

In an interview with Qatari newspaper Al Watan, Sheikh Nasser bin Faisal Al Thani, Al Jazeera Media Network director general, explained the philosophical necessity behind the expansion.

“From the very beginning, Al Jazeera was more than just another television channel,” Sheikh Nasser said. “It was a broader project to deepen public understanding.”

He said the strategy for the network’s fourth decade would be guided by three principles.

“Our fourth decade will be defined by three priorities: immediacy, understanding and the human dimension,” he said.

Under the new structure, each of Al Jazeera’s three Arabic-language news channels will have a distinct editorial focus.

Al Jazeera Mubasher, which began broadcasting in 2005, will continue its concentration on uninterrupted live coverage of events, without commentary from presenters or correspondents.

For breaking developments, the new Al Jazeera Now service will focus on developments as they unfold. But unlike a conventional news channel, it will operate without scheduled bulletins or a fixed programme grid.

Meanwhile, the flagship Al Jazeera Arabic channel will retain its news bulletins while pivoting more towards in-depth analysis and investigative journalism, as well as other programmes.

The restructuring is accompanied by plans for 33 programmes, promoted under the slogan “Your questions are our questions”.

Sheikh Nasser said the expansion was intended to provide more context on news events to Arab viewers.

“The real competitor today is not another channel, but noise – the flood of information that makes understanding harder, not easier,” he said, adding that Al Jazeera wanted to fill that gap in understanding.

Hamidi said the new programming would include investigative documentaries, discussions of political and social issues, and programmes examining the historical roots of current conflicts.

The network’s ambitions extend beyond television broadcasting to strengthening Al Jazeera’s local and regional reporting through dedicated digital platforms covering Palestine, Egypt, Sudan, the Gulf and other parts of the Arab world.

The Syria Now platform, which offers documentaries, investigations, and field reporting focused on Syrian affairs, has quickly emerged as one of the primary digital outlets for news on the country.

Looking ahead, the network is also planning a project called Al Jazeera Cultural, provisionally scheduled for launch in late 2027.

The initiative will serve as a space to foster sustained debate about the Arab world’s cultural and intellectual life.

The expansion also forms part of a wider technological transformation, including the development of The Core , an artificial intelligence initiative announced in December 2025 in collaboration with Google Cloud.

The initiative aims to integrate AI into newsroom operations, helping journalists manage information, coordinate coverage and make better use of the network’s reporting archives.

One component, Orbit, is being designed to coordinate newsroom workflows, including monitoring developments, commissioning stories, organising interviews, translating material and managing reporting assignments.

Sheikh Nasser said the first phase of The Core is scheduled to launch on November 1.

Despite the increased use of AI, Sheikh Nasser insisted that human oversight would remain primary.

“Artificial intelligence enables the human and does not replace him,” Sheikh Nasser said. “The main standard for us is conscience and editorial judgement, and editorial judgement is human.”
